transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-06-03 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miles, Priya Desai (Redwood); Dr. Aaron Kline, Maya Singh, Liam O'Connor (Nightingale Labs)

Summary: Quick readout on POC benchmark comparing Redwood runtime to incumbent baseline. We go through p50/p95/p99, talk about throughput with batching, routing fallbacks, and a strange quantization artifact on long clinical notes. Action items and lab scheduling at end.

[00:00] Jordan Miles: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on a Wednesday afternoon. Quick sanity check — audio ok for folks?
[00:05] Maya Singh: Yep can hear you, loud and clear.
[00:08] Jordan Miles: Great. I'll kick us off with a short agenda: readout of the latest bench numbers, discuss routing/fallback changes we proposed, dig into quantization artifacts Dr. Kline mentioned, and align on next steps. Priya will cover the more technical bits.
[00:22] Priya Desai: Hi all. I pulled the run from yesterday's lab. We ran the same prompt set the customer provided and matched request concurrency to the baseline test as close as possible. Two variants from Redwood: a default FP16 path with KV cache enabled and a quantized int8 path we tested for cost delta.
[00:40] Dr. Aaron Kline: Quick needed context — baseline is CloudGen AI with their managed endpoints, we see p95 around 230 ms and p99 spikes to ~580 ms on our production mix. Cost per 1k reqs is about $12 on their pricing.
[01:05] Priya Desai: Thanks Aaron. Our summarized numbers: p50 ~35 ms, p95 ~120 ms, p99 ~340 ms on the FP16 path when using Redwood hosted runtime with continuous batching tuned to your observed seq lengths. Throughput in the steady-state test was ~280 reqs/sec for the 2xA100 equivalent config we simulated locally.
[01:30] Liam O'Connor: So p95 is roughly half of baseline, p99 still high but better. What's the delta that causes the p99 spikes?
[01:40] Priya Desai: The main contributors are cold KV cache misses when requests land on different workers and occasional kernel fallbacks on long prompts that exceed the fast path. We saw about 12% of requests crossing the long-seq threshold which pushes execution to a slower attention kernel.
[01:58] Jordan Miles: To clarify, long prompts are primarily clinical notes that run past 2k tokens, right Aaron?
[02:05] Dr. Aaron Kline: Correct. Many discharge summaries and multi-section notes go 2k–4k tokens. Those are nontrivial and are where we saw the quantized int8 artefacts — some hallucination-like truncation on the final lines in the int8 runs.
[02:25] Priya Desai: Right, on int8 we saw a small increase in token error rate on the generation tail for >3k contexts. We've got a few mitigations: prefix KV caching pinned to session affinity, or routing long-context requests to the FP16 variant to avoid the int8 fast-path artifact.
[02:45] Maya Singh: Session affinity — what are the tradeoffs? We care about horizontal scale and not losing throughput.
[02:53] Priya Desai: Affinity reduces cache misses and dramatically lowers p99, but it reduces the global packing opportunities for batching across sessions. So p50/p95 improves for those long sessions, but overall throughput can drop if too many workers are pinned. We can implement heuristics: affinity only for requests exceeding 2.5k tokens and with a TTL of 10 minutes. That way bursts get benefit but normal short requests still pool.
[03:20] Jordan Miles: We tested that heuristic in sandbox and saw p99 drop from 340 ms to ~220 ms with affinity on long sessions, while overall throughput fell only 7% in our synthetic mix.
[03:33] Dr. Aaron Kline: That sounds promising. What about cost implications between FP16 and int8?
[03:40] Priya Desai: In our runs, int8 reduced average token compute cost by roughly 35% but introduced the tail risk on very long contexts. Mixed policy — route short/medium contexts to int8 and long contexts to FP16 — achieves about 20% cost savings overall vs baseline while keeping p99 within your target range.
[04:03] Liam O'Connor: Would that be automatic routing on our side or policy we set in Redwood?
[04:09] Jordan Miles: We can push a routing policy template and you can operate it from the console. It supports conditions: token_count > X, model_variant = int8, fallback = FP16, and region preference. Priya can show an example.
[04:24] Priya Desai: I'll share a sample policy after the call. Quick demo: it's a JSON-like policy but for the console we have a UI. You can set priorities and a weighted fallback.
[04:35] [05:00] (brief cross-talk, jam with screen)
[05:10] Maya Singh: On throughput — your 280 reqs/sec baseline, how does that scale if we add more workers or change batching windows? We can't afford latency regressions during peak bursts.
[05:25] Priya Desai: Batching window tuning is key. For your median token lengths (about 120 tokens), we get high packing and near-linear throughput scaling. If we increase batching window by 10 ms, throughput improves ~8% but p50 increases ~5 ms. We can expose a safe envelope so you can trade latency for throughput.
[05:50] Jordan Miles: We also tested an autoscale policy for dedicated slot that adds temporary burst capacity; Redwood's dedicated slot can be configured to add 1.5x burst capacity for up to 10 minutes. That keeps tail under control during spikes.
[06:06] Dr. Aaron Kline: Ok — one odd thing: in one of the int8 runs we saw truncated outputs where the final sentence got cut mid-word about 2% of the time. Is that a quantization glitch or a decoder timeout?
[06:20] Priya Desai: Our hypothesis is that it's a combination of two things — slight divergence in logits due to quantization rounding in the attention kernel, and a tokenization boundary mismatch in the prompt preprocessor for very long contexts. We reproduced it locally and added a guard to force FP16 on sequences that hit the boundary; that eliminated the truncation in our test run.
[06:41] Maya Singh: That will probably be fine as long as it doesn't change semantics. We need to see examples. Can you share 10 failure cases?
[06:48] Jordan Miles: Yes — ACTION ITEM: we will export the 10 failure transcripts and include model outputs across FP16 and int8 for comparison.
[06:55] [07:00] Jordan Miles: Next, a quick look at the raw numbers I sent in the sheet. (screen share) p50/p95/p99 table: Baseline (CloudGen) — p50 45 ms, p95 230 ms, p99 580 ms. Redwood FP16 — p50 35 ms, p95 120 ms, p99 340 ms. Redwood int8 mixed policy — p50 30 ms, p95 140 ms, p99 410 ms. Throughput: baseline steady 260 reqs/sec, Redwood 280 reqs/sec on our config.
[07:30] Liam O'Connor: These are encouraging. How confident are you these numbers map to our prod traffic, not just the synthetic bench?
[07:38] Priya Desai: We ran two validation passes: 1) replay of a day of production traffic with exact traffic mix and sticky sessions, 2) a stress run with amplified concurrency to test tail behavior. The replay matched the p95/p99 deltas within ~10%. Stress run exposed the quantization edge cases.
[07:58] Dr. Aaron Kline: Good. What's the plan to validate cost assumptions? We need ledger-level numbers for finance.
[08:06] Jordan Miles: We'll include estimated cost per 1k requests for each config in the sheet. For Redwood mixed routing we estimate $8.5 per 1k requests compared to CloudGen at $12 per 1k (approx). That's before reserved capacity discounts.
[08:24] Maya Singh: If we go to Dedicated, what pricing floor can we expect? Our procurement wants ballpark numbers for a 6-month pilot with expected 25M requests/month.
[08:33] Jordan Miles: I'll follow up with a ballpark: dedicated reserved nodes would drop unit cost significantly; I'll include a 6-month reserved quote in the pricing doc — ACTION ITEM: Jordan to send a pilot quote.
[08:45] Priya Desai: On the routing technical side, one more recommendation: enable per-route prefix caching for high-volume patient lookup prompts. That reduced repeated prefix recomputation and improved throughput for those routes by ~18% in our tests.
[09:03] Maya Singh: That is interesting — can that be applied selectively per route via the console?
[09:08] Priya Desai: Yes, you can apply cache hints on a per-route basis. We'll share a route config example.
[09:15] [09:30] (short pause while exchanging links)
[09:40] Dr. Aaron Kline: Let's talk acceptance criteria. For us, primary metrics are: p95 < 200 ms for standard workflows, p99 < 400 ms for long-context workflows, and no more than 0.5% quality regressions observed by our clinical review. If you can hit that, finance will be happy.
[10:02] Jordan Miles: That seems achievable with the mixed routing + affinity heuristic. We'll aim for p95 < 180 ms in the lab run.
[10:10] Liam O'Connor: One operational ask — audit logs for inference calls. We need request-level metadata in a format we can ingest.
[10:18] Priya Desai: Redwood can export request traces and per-token cost breakouts to your S3. We can provide a streaming audit log or daily batch. We'll include a sample schema in the security packet.
[10:31] Maya Singh: Also need SSO SAML integration and RBAC so only certain teams can access the dedicated slot.
[10:38] Jordan Miles: Yep — we have an integration guide. Jordan to attach the security and SSO instructions after the call.
[10:45] [11:00] (customer side background noise, brief interruption)
[11:15] Maya Singh: For the 99th percentile lab run, what's the recommended setup? We want to reproduce worst-case tails.
[11:22] Priya Desai: Two-phase test: A replay phase that uses your actual session affinity and prompt set at production concurrency, then a stress phase where we amplify concurrent short bursts and long-context interleaving. We'll provision a temporary dedicated slot equal to the pilot target capacity and run for 90 minutes. This will surface p99 and resource contention.
[11:45] Dr. Aaron Kline: Good. If we see regressions, do you have a quick rollback plan?
[11:50] Priya Desai: Yes — automatic fallback to baseline model variant or to FP16 within the same runtime. Console allows immediate rollback of routing and quantization policies. We'll test rollback in the lab window.
[12:04] Jordan Miles: Ok let's lock dates. Maya, Aaron — does 6/8 morning US time work for a 2-hour block?
[12:12] Maya Singh: 6/8 morning works for me. Aaron and Liam confirm?
[12:18] Dr. Aaron Kline: Works for me. Liam O'Connor: fine, set it up.
[12:22] Jordan Miles: Great. Actions recap: Jordan send benchmark CSVs, failure cases, pricing/quote; Priya send routing and policy examples plus route config; Maya provide prompt set and production profile. Then lab on 2026-06-08.
[12:40] Maya Singh: Quick question — can we get a temporary test token with increased rate limits to run the stress pass?
[12:46] Jordan Miles: Yes we can provision that; I'll include token and dedicated slot details in the email.
[12:52] Dr. Aaron Kline: Cool, thanks. Anything else before we wrap?
[12:56] Priya Desai: I'll attach the short checklist for the lab run and sample JMeter script we used.
[13:05] Jordan Miles: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in the email with attachments and schedule.
[13:10] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional timestamps every 20–60s; minor speaker attribution noise; disfluencies present.
